cards.front: What does it mean for code to be compiled against a library?
cards.back: That its class files hold direct references to that library's classes, members and descriptors — not to its source
cards.extra: The compiler writes the library's class name, member name and descriptor into the caller's constant pool. At run time the JVM resolves those references again; it never re-reads the library's source. So a library may change only in ways that keep those references resolvable and meaning the same thing.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What is a member's descriptor in a class file?
cards.back: The encoded parameter types and return type — part of the reference, not a comment
cards.extra: String quux(int, char) becomes quux(IC)Ljava/lang/String;. A caller's reference is name + descriptor, so changing parameter types or the return type leaves that reference dangling even though the source still compiles.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Which part of a public method's declaration can a library change without breaking binaries compiled against it?
cards.back: Only the body — name, parameters and return type are frozen by every existing caller
cards.extra: Rewriting a body is the most common release change and always binary compatible; JLS §13 lists reimplementing methods to improve performance. What the code does can still break behaviour, but never linkage.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: A library renames foo() to bar() and changes nothing else. What happens to code compiled against the old version?
cards.back: NoSuchMethodError when that call site is linked
cards.extra: Nothing in the caller's source is wrong, so nobody sees the problem until the class is linked at run time. Deleting or renaming a public method is the classic binary incompatibility.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: A library changes a method's return type only, leaving name and parameters untouched. Is that binary compatible?
cards.back: No — the return type is part of the descriptor, so old call sites no longer match
cards.extra: The caller holds quux(I)Ljava/lang/String;. Change the return type to Integer and the library declares quux(I)Ljava/lang/Integer;: the old reference resolves to nothing and throws NoSuchMethodError. Sources compile; binaries do not link.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: A public field changes type from int size to long size under the same name. Can old binaries still resolve it?
cards.back: No — a field reference is name + type, so it fails exactly like a removed field
cards.extra: The caller's descriptor says size:I, the library now declares size:J. Same name, different reference. This is why changing a field's type is treated as deleting and re-adding it.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why is deleting a private member binary compatible?
cards.back: No other class can hold a reference to it, so no pre-existing binary can depend on it
cards.extra: JLS §13 permits deleting private fields, methods and constructors outright. The same reasoning covers package-private members when the whole package ships together: only code inside that package could have referenced them.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why is moving a method up the class hierarchy binary compatible?
cards.back: Resolution walks the superclass chain, so the same name + descriptor is still found
cards.extra: A call site records 'invoke m on type C'; the JVM searches C and then its superclasses. Pulling m into a superclass — or inserting a new type into the hierarchy — keeps that search successful.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why does reordering fields or methods inside a class break nothing?
cards.back: References are by name + descriptor, never by position
cards.extra: The class file carries an index, so declaration order is not part of any reference. JLS §13 lists reordering declarations as binary compatible, which is why you can reorder source for readability.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Why does adding an overload preserve compatibility when changing the existing signature does not?
cards.back: The old descriptor still exists for old binaries, while new code binds to the new one
cards.extra: This is the standard evolution idiom: keep quux(int), add quux(long) and delegate to it. Changing quux(int) in place deletes a reference callers already hold — a break you can never reproduce on your own machine if you always rebuild.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: A method flips from static to an instance method with the same name and parameters. Is that binary compatible?
cards.back: Not guaranteed — JLS §13.4.12 says a linkage error may occur
cards.extra: The reference records whether the invocation is static or virtual, and the bytecode differs (invokestatic versus invokevirtual). Keeping the descriptor while changing the modifier leaves an opcode that no longer matches the member.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: Is narrowing a member's accessibility (public → protected) binary compatible?
cards.back: No — a pre-existing binary that no longer has access fails with IllegalAccessError
cards.extra: Access is checked during resolution, against the actual calling class. Widening is safe because anything that linked before still links; narrowing is not, even though the member itself still exists with the same descriptor.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does an API is a contract mean, in binary terms?
cards.back: A promise to binaries you do not control, not to the source you can recompile
cards.extra: Rebuild every dependent and most signature changes look harmless — which is why the break stays invisible in your own repo. The contract is with the class files already shipped: they can only be satisfied by name and descriptor stability.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals
